text:
Dow Slides Ahead of G-20 as Apple Dips, General Motors Falls By Nov. 30, 2018 8:29 a.m. ET Order Reprints Illustration by Michael Haddad Text size
Wheels Up. President Donald Trump flew to Argentina Thursday and now all eyes look to Argentina where he will meet with Chinese President Xi Jinping to discuss trade over dinner. Global equities are in the red this morning as investors fret about trade scenarios. Dow Jones Industrial Average futures are 137 points, or 0.5%, lower, S&P 500 futures have dipped 0.5% as well and Nasdaq Composite futures have dropped 0.4%. In today’s Morning Movers, we... ...prep for the G-20; ...look at some car stocks; ...and think about December. Barron’s Briefs G-20 Summit Standoff. Well, it’s finally here , and just about anything could happen. Comments from U.S. officials have indicated there may be a trade deal. Or maybe not. There has been a consistent theme with investors though—they expect a deal before they have to adjust 2019 numbers. Tariffs, intellectual property , and open markets are all on the table for discussion. No trade deal will equal more stock volatility in December, but trade-detente could be what the market needs to kick off a Santa rally . Retailers , industrial companies , and Apple (AAPL)-- threatened with iPhone tariffs —are the stocks that are most affected by the trade conflict. Shares of Apple have dipped 0.2% to $179.17. Automobile Apocalypse. HSBC cut estimates for European auto stocks, which has the sector down over 2% in Europe. Uncertainties abound: tariffs have been threatened, General Motors (GM) has been chastised in tweets , and car sales have slowed down in China . But all this is probably reflected in stock prices. The European Automobiles & Parts Index has slumped 24% in 2018, and trades for about 7 times earnings, roughly half the valuation of the European market as a whole. Shares of General Motors have fallen 1% to $36.40. Where Did 2018 Go? December is upon us and that means auto sales get reported Monday—along with other economic data. Industry data provider Ward’s expects the car annualized selling rate to stay above 17 million. Then at the end of next week OPEC meets. Predicting the outcome of that meeting is as difficult as calling the G-20 trade scenarios. OPEC was expected to cut output , but that will upset President Trump. After rising about 2% yesterday, oil is down about 1.8% this morning but still trades over $50 a barrel. For the week, U.S. crude future have risen a penny as of this writing. Tibor Kárpáti
